title: The Psalms
lead: The 150 songs and prayers of Israel's book of Psalms, with the psalms found elsewhere in the Bible and beyond it: how they were collected, sung and prayed, and how Jews and Christians have read them.

sections.h: Psalms outside the book of Psalms
sections.b: Israel sang long before the Psalter was gathered. The Song of the Sea (Exodus 15), the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32), the Song of Deborah (Judges 5), Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 2:1–10), David's laments for Saul and Jonathan and for Abner (2 Samuel 1:19–27; 2 Samuel 3:33–34) and Jonah's prayer (Jonah 2) are psalms in all but name. Two psalms appear twice in narrative books: Psalm 18 as 2 Samuel 22, and parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106 in the song of 1 Chronicles 16:8–36. Hezekiah's prayer (Isaiah 38:10–20) and Habakkuk 3, with its Selah and its note "for the music director," show the same forms used by prophets. In the New Testament, the songs of Mary, Zechariah and Simeon (Luke 1:46–55; Luke 1:68–79; Luke 2:29–32) are woven from psalm phrases.

sections.h: How the Psalter was put together
sections.b: The book is a collection of collections. Smaller groups can still be seen: psalms "of David" (3–41; 51–72; 138–145), of the sons of Korah (42–49; 84–88), of Asaph (50; 73–83), the Songs of Ascents (120–134), and the Hallelujah psalms (111–118; 146–150). Psalms 42–83 prefer the name Elohim, "God," to YHWH, which is why Psalm 14 and Psalm 53 differ (see Psalm 14:2). Psalm 72:20, "Here end the prayers of David son of Jesse," was once the end of a David collection, though more David psalms follow. The five books, each closed by a blessing (Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18–19; Psalm 89:52; Psalm 106:48), and the opening pair Psalms 1–2, show a final editing, which most scholars date to the Persian or early Greek period. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Psalms are the book found in the most copies (about forty, from Qumran, Masada and Nahal Hever; as reported), and the Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 (11QPs-a; as reported in Sanders' edition) has psalms of Books IV–V in a different order, mixed with other poems, including Psalm 151. Scholars debate whether it is a variant edition of the Psalter or a book of worship drawn from it.

sections.b: Hermann Gunkel (1920s–1930s) sorted the psalms by type, and most scholars still use his categories: hymns of praise (8; 29; 104), individual laments (3–7; 13; 22), communal laments (44; 74; 79), thanksgivings (30; 34; 116), royal psalms about the king (2; 18; 20–21; 45; 72; 110), songs of Zion (46; 48; 76; 84; 87; 122), wisdom and law psalms (1; 37; 49; 73; 119), songs of trust (11; 16; 23; 62) and entrance liturgies (15; 24). Sigmund Mowinckel tied many of them to festivals in the temple, including a yearly celebration of the LORD's kingship (47; 93; 95–99), a theory still debated. Laments, the largest group, usually move from complaint to trust and praise (13; 22).

sections.h: The Psalms in Jewish and Christian prayer
sections.b: The Levites sang a psalm for each day of the week at the daily offering in the Second Temple (Mishnah Tamid 7:4), and the Hallel (113–118) was sung at the festivals and at Passover (compare Mark 14:26). In the synagogue and the Jewish prayer book, psalms open the morning service (145–150), mark the Sabbath (92), the dead and the sick, and Psalm 145 is said three times daily (Bavli Berakhot 4b). Christians have sung psalms from the start (1 Corinthians 14:26; Colossians 3:16; Ephesians 5:19). Monks recited all 150 each week (Rule of Benedict 18), and the Liturgy of the Hours now spreads them over four weeks; the Anglican Book of Common Prayer over a month. Reformed churches put the psalms into metrical verse to sing, and some churches still sing only psalms in worship.

sections.h: The Psalms in the New Testament
sections.b: The New Testament quotes the Psalms more than any other Old Testament book. The most quoted verses are royal: Psalm 110:1 ("sit at my right hand"), Psalm 2:7 ("You are my son"), and Psalm 118:22 (the rejected stone). Jesus prays Psalm 22:1 and Psalm 31:5 on the cross. Peter and Paul read Psalm 16:8–11 of the resurrection (Acts 2:25–32; Acts 13:35), Hebrews reads Psalm 8:4–6 of Jesus (Hebrews 2:6–9), and Paul builds his case that all are under sin from Psalms 14, 5, 10, 140 and 36 (Romans 3:10–18). Jewish interpreters, from the rabbis to the medieval commentators, read the same psalms of David, of Israel, or of the Messiah still to come; see the topic on the Messiah.
